Knobbedlip fairy shrimp (Eubranchipus bundyi) is a vernal pool specialist that emerges from dormant resting eggs shortly after winter snowmelt, encountering rapidly warming waters that drive its development. Upon hatching, the free-swimming nauplius larva measures just 0.114 cm [Lb = 0.114 cm] in total length at birth, a diminutive size that reflects the limited yolk reserves packaged into the subitaneous egg. This initial length is remarkably small even by anostracan standards, though it allows the newly emerged larva to begin filter feeding on phytoplankton and bacteria almost immediately after yolk-sac resorption. The wet weight at birth has been calculated from the mean egg diameter of 0.34 mm, yielding an estimated value of 0.0000206 grams [Wwb = 0.0000206 grams], a mass that underscores the extreme energetic constraints operating during the earliest life stages. Such a tiny body mass imposes a high surface-area-to-volume ratio, necessitating rapid ingestion rates to meet basal maintenance requirements in the thermally dynamic pool environment.

Once the nauplius transitions through several instars, the growing juvenile enters a phase of accelerated somatic growth that culminates in the attainment of sexual maturity. At this key developmental threshold, individuals reach a total length at puberty of 0.65 cm [Lp = 0.65 cm], a size that is approximately 5.7 times the neonatal length but still less than half the ultimate adult body size. This measurement was confirmed through laboratory rearing experiments in which individual growth trajectories were tracked from the metanauplius stage onward. The onset of gonad maturation is tightly coupled to this body size threshold, with the first ovigerous females appearing only after passing the 0.65 cm mark. Males also attain reproductive maturity at a similar length, though they typically arrest somatic growth somewhat earlier than females. The coordination between size and reproductive activation is a common pattern among branchiopods, ensuring that individuals do not divert resources toward egg production before accumulating sufficient structural mass.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the life span of Eubranchipus bundyi is approximately 45.0 days [am = approximately 45.0 days], a relatively abbreviated adult duration that is characteristic of ephemeral pool anostracans. This maximum longevity is strongly temperature-dependent, as the metabolic costs of sustained swimming and filter feeding accelerate senescence at higher temperatures. Field-based observations generally corroborate this laboratory estimate, with most adults perishing within six to eight weeks of pool inundation as the water body dries or becomes hypoxic. The post-reproductive mortality that follows the final egg clutch deposition is rapid, with brooding females often dying within days of releasing their offspring. Such a compressed lifespan imposes strong selective pressure on early reproduction and rapid clutch production, as individuals have only a narrow temporal window in which to contribute offspring to the resting egg bank.

The ultimate total length, representing the maximum body size attained by fully grown adults, reaches 1.38 cm [Li = 1.38 cm] in this species under optimal conditions. This measurement was derived from a large series of preserved individuals collected from vernal pools in the eastern United States, where the species is most abundant. Females tend to achieve slightly larger sizes than males on average, a pattern that is common among fairy shrimps and that likely reflects the energetic demands of egg production and brooding. The corresponding ultimate dry weight calculated from this length and the condition factor is 0.00196 grams , a value that places Eubranchipus bundyi among the smaller-bodied members of its genus. The transition from the 0.65 cm pubertal length to the 1.38 cm adult maximum represents a doubling of body length, accompanied by a roughly tenfold increase in dry mass, illustrating the substantial investment in structural growth that occurs during the post-pubertal adult phase.

Comparative studies of lifetime reproductive output in this species have revealed that females produce a single clutch of subitaneous eggs per reproductive event, with clutch sizes ranging from 15 to 40 eggs depending on female body size and nutritional condition at the time of egg production [N_R_i = clutch sizes ranging from 15 to 40 eggs depending on female body size and nutritional condition at the time of egg production]. Females typically produce only a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], as the ephemeral nature of their pool habitat precludes multiple spawning bouts within a single season. This low frequency of reproduction, combined with small clutch sizes, is compensated by the production of robust resting eggs that can remain viable in the sediment for several years, acting as a bet-hedging strategy against unpredictable hydroperiods. The reproductive timing is tightly synchronized with the thermal regime of the pool, with the first clutch appearing approximately three weeks after the attainment of the 0.65 cm pubertal length. Adults at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] allocate most of their assimilated resources toward egg production rather than continued somatic growth, as their 45.0 day [am = 45.0 day] lifespan provides limited opportunity for iteroparity.
